prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) concept for future air traffic management (ATM) in the National Airspace System (NAS). Current NAS: the ATM system holds a predicted trajectory per flight from the approved flight plan plus a scheduled or controlled departure time. After movement, controllers tactically manage aircraft via 'open trajectory' vectors, altitude changes and speed clearances to implement traffic management restrictions, separate conflicting aircraft and address NAS constraints. Strategic changes are made via flight plan changes but are conservative, so many problems (weather reroutes, new Traffic Flow Management (TFM) restrictions) are left to controllers. Tactical controller actions are not communicated to automation systems or other stakeholders. Together with gaps in trajectory prediction data and models, this degrades prediction of constraint impacts and of NAS demand at each NAS resource. Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times to meet a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at a NAS constraint, based on the airspace user's estimated time en route but without knowledge of controller actions. Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) likewise assumes estimated times of arrival (ETAs) to the constraint are correct, although disruptions add unexpected delays. MBT: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights that respect airspace user goals while complying with NAS constraints. Negotiated 4DTs are used to communicate the traffic management plan. The concept accounts for both FAA and airspace user objectives and is flexible across airspace user types and trajectory characteristics. Actors so far: FAA, airspace users, controllers, ATM automation systems, other stakeholders.

New part:
U0013: As a result, the baseline concept accommodates a broad and expanding spectrum of current and anticipated airspace operations, from traditional commercial aviation to emerging users such as Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, and on-demand air transportation vehicles.
U0014: Pilots and air traffic controllers use automation to keep the aircraft on its assigned trajectory, which includes complying with temporal or speed constraints.
U0015: Equipped aircraft have substantial responsibility for complying with the assigned trajectory without controller intervention.
U0016: Assigned trajectories are constructed to respect all of the known constraints from the aircraft’s current location to its destination, making the flight’s entire trajectory much more predictable than it is today.
U0017: Where uncertainty or disruptions occur, resolutions are, to the extent possible, handled through trajectory modifications as far in advance as possible.
U0018: Future improvements in automation (ground-based and aircraft) and data communications (air-ground and among stakeholders on the ground) make the MBT concept possible.
U0019: MBT eliminates most local, reactive control actions being applied to aircraft, which cannot be predicted in advance and which have impacts on the downstream trajectory that cannot be known until they happen.
U0020: MBT does this by inserting the impact of all NAS constraints into the assigned trajectory in the form of trajectory constraints.
U0021: Where uncertainty remains, necessary adjustments to the trajectory constraints are made proactively, maximizing trajectory predictability and delivering associated benefits. 1 In this way, MBT is similar to Trajectory Based Operations concepts that employ a 4D contract.
U0022: The appendix “Comparison with ICAO TBO Concept” compares MBT with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO concept.
U0023: In the past decade, the term Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) has been used widely.
U0024: The term TBO has come to be used in two distinct ways.
U0025: One meaning of TBO is as a high-level vision for the future of the NAS in which 4DTs are the core of air traffic control and air traffic management.
U0026: The second meaning of TBO is an evolving set of specific endeavors intended to advance the NAS toward the future vision.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
